Zorn's Lemma

Stand the divisors of twelve in divisibility order. Climb a chain and see what sits at the top.

A chain is a line of mutually comparable elements. If every chain has an upper bound, a maximal element exists. You never construct it; existence is guaranteed. The guarantee matches the axiom of choice.

For example, the top of a 🪜 staircase has no next step. Every way up ends somewhere. Knowing every climb ends proves a top exists.

every chain has an upper bound⇒∃ maximal m\text{every chain has an upper bound} \Rightarrow \exists\, \text{maximal } mevery chain has an upper bound⇒∃maximal m
1∣2∣4∣12,1∣3∣6∣121 \mid 2 \mid 4 \mid 12,\quad 1 \mid 3 \mid 6 \mid 121∣2∣4∣12,1∣3∣6∣12

Examples & Exercises

Prove that every nonempty finite poset has a maximal element (the finite version of Zorn's lemma — no choice axiom needed).

P≠∅ finite poset ⇒ ∃ m∈P maximalP \ne \varnothing\ \text{finite poset} \ \Rightarrow\ \exists\, m \in P\ \text{maximal}P=∅ finite poset ⇒ ∃m∈P maximal
Show proof

  1. Let PPP be a nonempty finite poset. Pick any x0∈Px_0 \in Px0​∈P. If x0x_0x0​ is maximal, we are done.

    Otherwise some x1∈Px_1 \in Px1​∈P with x0<x1x_0 < x_1x0​<x1​ exists (that is exactly what "x0x_0x0​ is not maximal" means).

  2. Repeat: if xkx_kxk​ is not maximal, pick xk+1x_{k+1}xk+1​ with xk<xk+1x_k < x_{k+1}xk​<xk+1​. The terms of x0<x1<x2<⋯x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdotsx0​<x1​<x2​<⋯ are all distinct (antisymmetry and transitivity give xi<xjx_i < x_jxi​<xj​ for i<ji < ji<j).

    But PPP is finite, so infinitely many distinct elements cannot be drawn.

  3. Hence the process must stop — some xkx_kxk​ is maximal. Finiteness making "climbing forever" impossible is the entire proof; for infinite posets this argument breaks, and Zorn's lemma (with the axiom of choice) is needed.

Concretely, for the three maximal chains: C0={1,2,4,12}C_0 = \{1,2,4,12\}C0​={1,2,4,12} has upper bounds {12}\{12\}{12}, C1={1,2,6,12}C_1 = \{1,2,6,12\}C1​={1,2,6,12} has {12}\{12\}{12}, C2={1,3,6,12}C_2 = \{1,3,6,12\}C2​={1,3,6,12} has {12}\{12\}{12} (an upper bound of a chain containing 12 must be a multiple of 12, and the only multiple of 12 in PPP is 12).     The only multiple of 12 in PPP is 12 itself, so 12 is maximal — and unique. Exactly as Zorn's lemma promises.
